sections.title: Cell morphology
sections.live: LIVE H2 → Closed Cell vs Open Cell · two cards, five metrics each — the best explanatory block on the site · one metric on the open-cell card is a measured acoustic value with no test behind it

fields.label: Eyebrow
fields.note: [no change]

fields.label: H2
fields.note: [no change — it is the literal comparison a buyer searches and it is correctly phrased]

fields.label: Intro
paragraphs: Specifying cell structure is the first decision in foam engineering. It controls water absorption, compression set, thermal resistance and acoustic performance simultaneously — which is why it comes before compound, not after it.
leads: It controls water absorption, compression set, thermal resistance and acoustic performance simultaneously
fields.note: 35 words · live is 26 · the live sentence is excellent and is kept whole. The closing clause is added because it states the ordering principle the section is demonstrating and never says out loud

fields.label: Card 1 — closed cell
rows: Low — recovers fully, to ASTM D395 Method B
fields.note: Five metrics, five metrics. One addition: compression set gains its test method, which Margo runs in-house and which section 08 already asks the buyer to state a criterion against. Naming it here connects the two blocks

fields.label: Card 2 — open cell
rows: Excellent — absorption rises with thickness and airflow resistance
fields.note: Five metrics, five metrics. The NRC figure comes off. Noise reduction coefficient is measured under ASTM C423 in a reverberation room, on a stated thickness and mounting — it is a property of a tested assembly, not of open-cell foam as a class, and Margo publishes no acoustic test capability anywhere. The replacement says more, not less: that absorption depends on thickness and airflow resistance is the thing an acoustic specifier actually needs to hear, and it opens the conversation the NRC number closed

notes: “closed cell vs open cell foam” is a high-volume informational search with a definite answer, and this block answers it better than most of the results that currently rank for it. It is the strongest AEO asset on this page and possibly on the site.
Both cards must be real markup, not images. Two five-row metric comparisons rendered as graphics publish nothing. <dl> pairs inside a <section> per card, with an <h3> for each structure name.

Give the block its own id and link to it. #cell-structure already exists. It should be linked from the gaskets page, the extrusion page and the industries pages — it is the explainer those pages assume and none of them has.
Do not put the density ranges in schema from this block. Section 05 is the canonical density statement; two machine-readable ranges on one page is one too many.

The removed NRC figure should not be replaced by any number until an acoustic test exists. If one is commissioned, the right claim names ASTM C423, the thickness and the mounting — and it would be genuinely differentiating, because no Indian competitor publishes one.

sections.title: Compound comparison
sections.live: LIVE H2 → All Five Compared · five rows, five columns · every service range differs from the homepage table — correctly, because sponge is not solid rubber · but the neoprene row is 25 °C above the published constant rating

fields.label: Eyebrow
fields.note: [no change]

fields.label: H2
fields.note: [no change — short, accurate, and it does not pretend to be a keyword]

fields.label: Table — 5 rows
rows: HVAC gaskets, roofing tape, weatherseals, hot-water systems
Marine seals, refrigerant lines, adhesive tape backing
Hydraulic seals, oil-resistant gaskets, fuel system foam
Anti-vibration mounts, acoustic panels, packaging foam
Clean-room seals, food-contact grades, high-temperature ovens
fields.note:
Hardness bands and full names are unchanged. The temperature column is rewritten on all five rows to state constant and intermittent separately — the distinction that matters on cellular rubber, because the cell structure degrades before the polymer does.
Neoprene is the substantive correction: live gives −40 to +100 °C; published closed-cell neoprene sponge to ASTM D1056 is −40 to +75 °C constant with excursions to +90. The live figure is 25 °C above the constant rating, and it is the row most likely to be misused — a refrigerant-line seal specified at +100 hardens in service.
EPDM and NBR upper limits move down to their constant ratings, with the live figures kept as the intermittent values, so nothing is lost.
The applications column changes on one row: silicone drops “medical devices” for “clean-room seals, food-contact grades” — see the FDA note above

fields.label: Footnote — new
paragraphs: Sponge grades carry lower service temperatures than the same compound in solid rubber. The cell structure degrades before the polymer does, so a closed-cell EPDM sponge is rated below a solid EPDM moulding — the figures above are cellular ratings to ASTM D1056 and are not the same as the solid-compound table published elsewhere on this site. Constant service is the figure to design to; intermittent covers short excursions, not duty. Density and cell structure both shift these limits, so confirm against the grade quoted for your part.
leads: Sponge grades carry lower service temperatures than the same compound in solid rubber.
fields.note: 83 words · live has no footnote at all · this paragraph is what stops the next consistency audit reading this table as drift. Nine category pages disagree with the homepage compound table by accident; this one disagrees on purpose, and until now nothing on the page said so. It also teaches the constant-versus-intermittent distinction, which is the single most misread thing in a rubber datasheet

notes: Real <table> markup with <caption>Sponge rubber compounds, hardness and cellular service temperature ranges</caption> and scope="col" on every header. All five rows in the DOM at first paint.

The constant / intermittent split is an AEO gain. “What temperature can EPDM foam take?” now returns two figures with a stated difference, which is a better answer than one number and is the shape a technical assistant prefers to cite.
This table and the tab panels in section 03 must render from one record. Two views, one source. The corrected values must appear in both or the page contradicts itself between two adjacent blocks.

The footnote is load-bearing for the whole site. It is the only place that explains why one product page legitimately disagrees with the homepage compound table. Without it, a future audit “corrects” this page back to the solid-rubber figures and publishes a neoprene sponge rated 45 °C above its constant limit.
Overflow. Five columns will not fit 375 px — overflow-x:auto on the wrapper, never on the body.

sections.title: Self-adhesive foam tape
sections.live: LIVE H2 → Self-Adhesive Foam Tape · cross-section build-up, two foam cores, two adhesive systems and a surface-energy engineering note — the most specialised block on the site · the intro claims a 40% assembly-time saving with nothing behind it

fields.label: Eyebrow
fields.note: [no change]

fields.label: H2
fields.note: [no change — it is the exact phrase a converter or panel builder searches, and it is the only place on the site that carries it]

fields.label: Intro
paragraphs: Pre-applied pressure-sensitive adhesive converts any foam compound into an instant-bond sealing tape. The assembly step it removes is the one that causes most field failures — a separately applied adhesive cures at whatever rate the line allows, on whatever surface preparation the operator had time for. A factory-laminated tape arrives with the bond already made.
leads: The assembly step it removes is the one that causes most field failures
fields.note: 56 words · live is 30 · “reducing assembly time by up to 40%” comes off. It is an up to percentage with no study, no customer and no measurement, and it is the only marketing-style claim on an otherwise expert page. The replacement argues the same benefit from the mechanism instead, which is both true and more persuasive to the engineer who has actually watched a hand-applied bead fail

fields.label: Cross-section build-up
fields.value:
Foam core (EPDM or CR)
Acrylic or rubber adhesive
Release liner (PE / silicone)
fields.note: [no change — three named layers in order is exactly right, and the release liner material is the kind of detail that tells a converter this supplier has made the product]

fields.label: Foam core comparison ×2
rows: Outdoor weatherseals, curtain-wall expansion joints, HVAC flanges
Marine hatches, refrigerant pipe wrap, fire-door perimeters
fields.note: Two cores, two cores — no count change. Both temperatures are brought into line with the corrected section 04 table, which is the point of correcting it: the neoprene figure appears twice on this page and fixing one and not the other would leave the contradiction in place. The refrigerant pipe wrap application makes the neoprene correction matter — that is precisely the duty where a 25 °C overstatement gets a seal specified into a line it cannot hold

fields.label: Adhesive comparison ×2
rows: High temperature resistance to +150 °C · excellent long-term bond durability · good UV and solvent resistance · slower tack, requires dwell time
Immediate high tack, instant bond · excellent peel strength on irregular surfaces · cost-effective for interior use · lower temperature ceiling, to +80 °C
fields.note: [no change to any value] — this comparison is correct as written and it is unusually honest. Each system is given a real disadvantage: acrylic needs dwell time, rubber has a lower ceiling. A page that tells a buyer the downside of both options is a page they trust on the upside

fields.label: Engineering note
paragraphs: Surface energy of the substrate determines adhesive selection. For low-surface-energy substrates such as PP, PE or powder-coated panels, specify acrylic adhesive with a primer or corona pre-treatment. For metals and glass, either system performs; rubber adhesive delivers superior initial grab.
fields.note: [no change] — the most specialised paragraph on this website. Surface energy is the actual reason foam tapes fail in the field, it is understood by almost nobody outside the adhesives trade, and no competing Indian supplier page mentions it. It should be given its own <h3> so it can be retrieved on its own

notes: This block deserves its own URL. self-adhesive foam tape manufacturer India, EPDM foam tape and acrylic vs rubber adhesive tape are three distinct searches with distinct buyers, and this section already contains a better page for all three than most of what ranks. It has an id already. Flagged as a scope decision, not built here — splitting it is a site-architecture change, not a copy change.

The engineering note is the citable passage. “Which adhesive for a low surface energy substrate?” has a precise answer here, with the pre-treatment named. Give it

Choosing an adhesive for your substrate

and it becomes independently retrievable.
The two comparison blocks must be real tables or <dl> pairs, not styled cards with loose text. Four attributes across two options is a comparison, and comparisons are what get extracted.
Do not put the +150 °C and +80 °C adhesive ceilings in schema. They are adhesive-system properties, not product properties, and a machine-readable figure here would be attributed to the foam.

The removed 40% claim should not be replaced by any percentage unless a customer measurement exists. If one does, name the customer and the process — an unattributed percentage is worth less than the mechanism argument that replaced it.
